chapters.label: Act I
chapters.title: Grief
paras: The world ended for me at 4:32 AM on a Wednesday. It didn’t end the way people think it would, with fiery skies, earthquakes, or some voice in the heavens declaring, "That’s enough, I’m shutting this circus down." No, it ended with a hand on my shoulder, the kind only a mother should give. But it wasn’t my mother.
It was Mariam. And her hand was trembling.

I woke up slowly, the way kids do, rolling onto my side, waiting for the sunlight to find me. But today felt wrong. The house smelled like burnt toast, though no one was making breakfast. The light through the curtains wasn’t golden; it was gray, like the sun had decided it wasn’t worth rising. And Mariam… Mariam never woke me up like this.
"Safiyah." Her voice shook. "Sweetheart, wake up."
I rubbed my eyes. She was kneeling beside my bed, lips pressed together so tightly they’d turned white. She smelled like sweat. She hadn’t showered.
She wasn’t looking at me. She was looking at the floor.
I sit up. "Where’s Mama?"
Mariam sucked in a breath, like she needed to borrow air before speaking. She tried to say something, but no words came out.

I looked past her, at the open bedroom door, as if I could will them into existence. Baba should have been in the hallway, grumbling about coffee. Mama should have been behind him, laughing, teasing him for being dramatic. But the house was silent.
Not quiet. Silent.
A cold hand brushed its fingers down my spine.

Mariam reached for my hands, gripping them tightly in hers. "Sweetheart, listen to me, okay?" Her voice cracked. "Your mama and baba—" She stopped, squeezed her eyes shut like she could erase the words before they came out. "The plane they were on crashed last night."
I blinked.
The words didn’t make sense. They felt like puzzle pieces from different boxes. Plane. Crashed. Last night.
Mariam kept talking, but I wasn’t listening anymore.
Mama had kissed me goodnight. Baba had promised to bring back a gift.
"What do you mean?" My voice was small.
Mariam’s chin trembled. "They’re… They’re not coming back, habibti."

I stared at her, waiting for her to take it back, to say she’d made a mistake. That any second now, Mama would walk in, complaining about the flight, Baba right behind her, carrying a bag of souvenirs.
But they never came. And outside, the world kept spinning.

Let’s pause here. Not for her. For you. I know what you're thinking. I see every thought, every emotion that rises inside you as you're reading this. You think this is cruel. That a child losing her parents overnight is a merciless hand to be dealt. And you’re right. It is merciless. It is unfair. It is the very thing that makes humans raise their fists to the sky and demand to know where I was when it all happened.

Contrary to atheists' views, I was there. I am always there. I watched her sleep peacefully while that happened and the news broke. I listened to the panic in Mariam’s prayers and felt her disappointment when they were unanswered. I felt the loss of those who depended on them. I knew, felt, and saw it all. And I still let it happen.
Why, you ask? You wouldn’t understand. Not yet. But let me tell you something; I have always been watching her.

From the moment she was born, screaming, pink, and furious at the world, I was there. From the first time she scraped her knee and looked up at the sky as though the heavens owed her an explanation, I was there. And now, as her world crumbles, I am still here.

You must understand that her story is only beginning. And before you throw in your accusations, before you let anger build in your heart, I should let someone else speak. Because he has been there watching too.
Oh, we’re doing introductions now? Fine. I’ll play along.
You. Yes, you. The one reading this. Let’s get something straight. You think you know me. Great! I have you fooled, just like I do most people.

You’ve given me many names, some poetic, some ridiculous, some downright offensive. The Devil! Adversary! The Morning Star... That last one? A mistake some guy made a long time ago, and somehow, it stuck.

For those of you who still haven't guessed it, I'm a man of many names, several forms, and multiple faces. Call me Haylel; I'm not Lucifer. I was the Light-Bringer, once, but that was a person I'm not anymore, in a time entirely left behind in the eons of your cosmos's history. Lucifer was a mistranslation turned myth, and now I'm saddled with a misconstrued legacy. But that’s how humans are, isn’t it? You lot rewrite the stories you fear the most into things your mind can comprehend.
But enough about me for now. Let’s talk about Safiyah.
I’ve been watching her too. Not the way He does. He has patience for y'all and this thing called purpose. Me? I've been watching out of curiosity, because, why not?

A child loses everything in a moment, and the world shifts beneath her feet. Hey, haven't we played that game before with Job? It's my favourite and I get to play it with most of y'all, because that’s where things get interesting.

It's so funny, it always cracks me up. Humans... oh, humans are something else. You throw grief at them, and their world turns upside down. And Safiyah? I guess I started the game now because she’s going to be something worth watching.
I observed that He's been watching her, and I knew he had a plan, so I thought to play my hand and see. I would like to claim this one.

Spoiler! Let’s not pretend this is going to be some delicate tale of innocence and healing where Safiyah will find hope and redemption in the end. No, this will be a story of suffering; one without hope in sight.

She will burn. She will rage. And I will be there to enjoy it all. Because no matter how much humans love to paint me as the villain, the truth is, they make their own choices. And this is a story of choices. All I'll do is bear witness.
So settle in for the horror. This is going to be one HELL of a story.

Grief doesn’t come all at once or manifest the same way for everyone. It’s not like how it's portrayed, where you hear bad news, fall to your knees, and scream at the sky, and everyone knows you're broken. No, grief is slow. It’s a shadow that stretches across your life, inch by inch, until one day, you look around and realize there’s no sunlight left.
At first, I thought the worst part was losing them. But I was wrong. Things kept getting worse.

It started when they began arriving the day after the funeral. Aunts, uncles, and cousins I’d never met before. They came with sad smiles and soft voices, their arms opening for hugs I didn’t want. They smelled like expensive perfume and something else rotten beneath.

At first, they were nice. They held my hand, stroked my hair, and told me I looked just like my mother. That they’d take care of me. That I had nothing to worry about. Then they started asking questions.
"Where is the will?"
"Who handled your late parents' accounts?"
"Did your father ever mention a safe?"
No one asked if I was okay being asked all of that, or if I was okay answering.
They sat in the living room with serious faces, talking in hushed voices while I sat on the staircase, knees pulled to my chest, listening to every word.
"This house is too big for her."
"It would be best if she stayed with family."
"She’s a child. She doesn’t need all that money just sitting there."
I didn’t say anything. I just pressed my forehead against my knees and counted my breaths. Five in. Five out. Don’t cry. Don’t make a sound.
Then, they started taking things.

First, it was small. A watch here, a necklace there. Then it was the paintings, the furniture, the things that had always been there, part of the house, part of us. My father’s books, my mother’s jewelry, the silk scarves she used to wrap her hair at night. One by one, they disappeared.
Mariam tried to stop them. She argued, yelled, and even grabbed my mother’s wedding ring out of one of my aunt’s hands. But Mariam was just the maid. And no one listens to the maid.
I think that’s when she knew we’d already lost.
The papers came last.

Some cousin I didn’t recognize showed up with documents, signatures, and legal words that didn’t mean anything to me. But I understood what they meant when Mariam’s face turned pale, when her hands clenched into fists at her sides.
They meant we had nothing left. No money. No house. No place to go.
By the time the last car pulled away, the house was empty. The walls were still there, the floors, the windows, but it wasn’t ours anymore. It was just another thing they had taken.
Mariam knelt in front of me, her hands gripping my shoulders. "I won’t leave you, habibti. I swear it."
I believed her. But I also knew that love isn’t enough to stop people from taking what they want.
I stood in the middle of what used to be our home, staring at the dust settling in the places where our things had been.
I didn’t cry. I didn’t scream. I just held Mariam’s hand and watched the last piece of my life disappear. And somewhere, deep inside, something small began to harden.
People say children don’t understand things like loss, corruption, or fear. They say we forget that we heal quickly, that we don’t see the world the way adults do. They’re wrong.
I knew, even before the papers were signed and the house was stripped bare, that there was no one coming to save me.

But Mariam tried. She held my hand tightly as we stepped into the lawyer’s office on the next Monday. It smelled like old books and coffee. The man behind the desk, Mr. Rafiq, had known my father for years. His eyes softened when he saw me, and for a moment, I believed he could help.
"Your father was a great man, Safiyah," he said, his voice sorrowful. "Your mother, too. It's a tragedy what happened to them. I promise you, we’ll make this right."
For the first time since the world ended, I felt like there was hope. But hope is a fragile thing. And it doesn’t last.
Three days later, Mr. Rafiq was dead. A car accident, they said. A tragedy. Just one of those things that happen.

His associate, a younger man with expensive shoes and cold eyes, took over his clients. Mariam and I went back to the office a week after, but this time, there was no warmth. No kindness. Just a man who barely looked at me as he flipped through the paperwork.
"I’m sorry, but there’s nothing I can do." His voice was insincere. Final.
Mariam argued. She pleaded. She reminded him that my father had trusted this firm. But the man only sighed, rubbing his temples like we were an inconvenience.
"The will is missing, the assets are already in dispute, and without proof of guardianship, I’m afraid there’s nothing legal to be done."

Nothing legal. I was six, but even I could hear what he was really saying. There was something illegal to be done. Something that might have been possible, for the right price, for the right people. But not for us.
Mariam gripped my hand and stormed out. I didn’t ask what she was thinking. I didn’t need to. I could feel the anger rolling off her, sharp and hot like the desert wind.
That night, I heard them talking.
Not Mariam. The others. The ones who had taken everything.
They thought I was asleep, curled up on the thin mattress Mariam had laid out for me in the guest room. But their voices slipped through the walls, low and cruel.
"You think this is over?" one of them muttered. "With the kind of enemies her parents had?"
"If something happens to the girl, it won’t be a surprise."
The air turned to ice in my lungs. I didn’t breathe. Didn’t move.
I wasn’t sure if they knew I was there. If they meant for me to hear. But it didn’t matter. The words were already inside me, curling in my chest like venomous vipers.
I waited until the voices faded, until I was sure they were gone. Then I slipped out of bed and ran to Mariam’s room.
She was awake. She didn’t ask why I was shaking. She just pulled me into her arms and held me tight.
"I heard them," I whispered. "They said if something happens to me—"
"Nothing will happen to you, habibti." Her voice was fierce. She cupped my face, forcing me to meet her eyes. "Do you hear me? Nothing. I won’t let them touch you."
I wanted to believe her. But I’d believed a lot of things before, and none of them had been true.
The next morning, Mariam packed a bag.
"We’re leaving."
"Where?" I asked.
"Home," she said.
Not my home. Hers.

Mariam didn’t have much. She had spent her life taking care of my family, and now, all she had was me. But she didn’t hesitate. She wrapped a scarf around my head, held my hand, and walked us out of that house for the last time.
No one stopped us. No one even noticed we were leaving. And for the first time since everything fell apart, I let myself wonder if maybe, just maybe, running was the only way to survive.

Mariam’s home was small, tucked away like folded sleeves into the edge of a neighborhood where the streets were narrow and the air smelled like spices and sun-warmed stone. It wasn’t like our house, not with its high ceilings and polished floors, not with its garden where Mama used to sit in the evenings, drinking tea and flinging me around with Baba. This place was different. It was smaller. It felt too constraining.

Mariam took me inside and led me to a room with a thin mattress and walls that had seen too many years. She placed a blanket over my shoulders, set a warm cup of tea in front of me, and told me to rest.
I didn’t. Instead, I sat on the bed, staring at the wall, feeling the burden of the last few weeks' everything settle into my bones.
Mama and Baba were gone. The house was gone. The life I had known, the soft, safe world built around me, was gone. What was left?

How was I supposed to live now? How would I go to school? Who would take care of me? Where would I go when Mariam couldn’t keep me anymore? Because I knew, even at six years old, that people like me who were called orphans were burdens and were never meant to stay in one place for long.
The thoughts came too fast, tangled together like a storm in my head, and for the first time since it happened, I couldn’t hold it in anymore. I broke.

The sobs came suddenly, the panic and grief overtaking my entire body, tearing through me like I was being ripped apart from the inside. My throat burned. My chest ached. I gasped for air, but it wasn’t enough, it was never enough—
And then, arms wrapped around me.
Mariam. She didn’t say anything. Didn’t tell me to stop or to be strong. She just held me, steady and warm, letting me fall apart in her arms.
"She is lost now, drowning in grief, saddled with questions she cannot answer about a life she's not even started living. And yet, even here, in this her darkness, she is not alone.

"Mariam has been there since the beginning, a constant in her life. She may not be the lighthouse that Safiyah's looking for, nor can she sweep away the pain or give the girl the kind of comfort she's looking for, but she is there. And sometimes, that is enough."
"Ah, but let’s not get sentimental now.
"When I told you I wasn't involved and was only watching out of curiosity, you really thought I was being honest? Oh, you poor gullible human, shame on you for believing me.

"It was all me. The plane crash. The whisper in the ears of relatives who saw an orphan girl as nothing more than an opportunity. The lawyer who was erased when he wanted to help. All of it was done by my influence. Every bit of it, carefully placed, beautifully executed. And now, look at her. Shattered and alone.
"I am proud of this one and of my handiwork. And let me tell you, I can’t wait to see what happens next."
